title: A Conversation About the Workverse, Human Judgment, AI, and Learning by Doing
author: Matt Hutson
summary: Matt Hutson condenses a conversation with Michelle Duval and Dan Negroni, authors of Find Your Workverse, about preparing young people for work when the old career ladder is unreliable. The discussion draws on a motivation study spanning 23 years and over 400,000 people, and recasts a career as a personal system of overlapping work, purpose and relationships. Hutson offers his CARE method (Clarify, Articulate, Refine, Execute) as a loop that turns uncertainty into small, testable experiments. On AI, the guests welcome student skepticism and argue that speed is not judgment, so humans must still decide, verify and take responsibility. The piece stresses confidence built through reps and suggests low-cost experiments such as talking to a practitioner or making a rough sample. It closes with advice for parents and educators to listen before advising and to hand teenagers real, small choices.
points: A career is better described as a personal system (a workverse) of work, purpose and relationships than as a single ladder.
The CARE method (Clarify, Articulate, Refine, Execute) frames learning as a loop of small, testable steps rather than a staircase.
AI can speed up options and critique, but humans must still decide, verify claims and own the result.
Confidence comes from repeated low-stakes reps, such as talking with a practitioner or making a rough sample.
Adults should listen before advising and give young people small real choices to practice judgment.
quotes: Our starting point was a large study of motivation and generational change. We looked across 23 years of data and more than 400,000 people, including about 83,000 Gen Z participants.

CARE stands for Clarify, Articulate, Refine, and Execute. We clarify what we’re trying to learn, articulate what we currently think, refine that thinking with new information and feedback, and execute by making or trying something tangible.
CARE is a loop, not a staircase. A first attempt may reveal that the question needs to change.
AI can help us move faster, but speed is not the same as judgment. It can suggest, summarize, or help us rehearse.
People rarely see the early versions—the first video, first post, or first attempt that didn’t work. Learning comes through reps.
Adults can provide structure, resources, and guardrails while handing over real choices.

We cannot hand young people a perfect map for a world that is still changing. We can help them understand themselves, ask better questions, build relationships, and learn through manageable experiments.
